rationale: One patient with diabetic neuropathy had syncope after a white-rice meal. The second test adds caffeine. The orthostatic tilt was separate and there is no brown-rice or meal-related standing-lightheadedness comparison.

Randomized crossover of full versus half a rice serving in 39 nursing-home residents reported less frequent postprandial hypotension with the half portion. Rice grade, exact estimates, posture and symptom results are unverified.

Rice cake and alcohol preceded loss of consciousness, with no event pressure, determined cause, rice-only contrast or orthostatic symptom rating. The author abstract event year and journal issue year conflict.
Review contrasts postprandial hypotension and orthostatic hypotension and discusses meal carbohydrate; no original brown rice or posture-specific symptom estimate in indexed abstract.
Review of postprandial versus orthostatic hypotension in older and Parkinson populations; no original brown rice intervention in abstract.
Same single diabetic white-rice case as BRR2 rank 1. The test distinguishes caffeine exposure, meal syncope, and a separate abnormal tilt.
Same 39-person full-versus-half rice study as BRR2 rank 2. Postprandial measurements do not establish a standing symptom effect.

32 cognitively healthy older adults had high-carbohydrate versus high-fat mixed breakfasts; seated or lying BP over four hours, 37.5% met PPH criterion. No isolated brown rice or standing symptom contrast.

23 older adults consumed oats, sultanas, milk and Polyjoule breakfast, seated throughout; 12 had PPH and three per group reported any dizziness or nausea, with no significant symptom group or time difference. No rice or orthostatic comparison.
Narrative carbohydrate intake review notes elderly post-meal hypotension; abstract provides no original food-specific or orthostatic symptom comparison.

Reproduced original crossover in the author's thesis. Twelve seated geriatric participants consumed three glucose-syrup loads. Hypotensive duration and overall symptom burden favored the low load. No brown rice or standing symptom contrast.
Hypothesis about glucose regulation and hypertension discusses high-carbohydrate post-meal pressure; no original brown rice or symptom outcome in abstract.

Ten older adults had carbohydrate, fat, and fat plus insulin meals; pressure fell 8–10 mmHg after carbohydrate and fat plus insulin, not fat alone. Supine baseline; no reported orthostatic symptoms or rice.

Ten healthy older people randomized across 50g glucose, sucrose, fructose and water; seated measurements, glucose and sucrose lowered BP versus fructose and water. No rice or orthostatic symptom comparison.

Eight untreated hypertensive older participants crossover meal versus no meal had greater supine and erect SBP falls but maintained orthostatic BP control; no rice or lightheadedness data in abstract.

Eight older patients with meal-related syncope compared to seven young and 12 older controls after a high-carbohydrate meal; mean pressure fell 26 versus 9 mmHg at 60 min in syncope versus older controls. Food composition and standing symptom tests unavailable in abstract.

64 untreated PD patients aged 70 or older: 75 g glucose challenge; orthostatic hypotension on separate tilt predicts post-glucose hypotension. No steamed brown rice or symptom severity contrast; already in 0760 ledger.

37 untreated PD and 10 controls: systolic decreases after 75 g oral glucose correlated with decrease on separate tilt r=0.359, p<0.05. No rice or standing-lightheadedness rating; existing ledger cohort.

113 PD patients underwent ambulatory monitoring and supine/standing office measurements; a classification algorithm includes postprandial hypotension but does not specify a rice intervention or symptom response. Nature original indexed body snippets retrieved; continuous full text inaccessible on redirect, so abstract depth only.
Clinical review discusses orthostatic hypotension and postprandial hypotension in parkinsonian disorders; no primary rice intervention or rice-specific symptom estimate in abstract.

Randomized crossover levodopa/benserazide versus placebo in 17 Parkinsonian patients assessed standardized standing and meal tests. Existing claim ledger describes two patients with post-meal symptoms and separate standing tests; no steamed rice contrast.
Review of autonomic failure in PD describes orthostatic and postprandial hypotension; not a primary food-specific trial or symptom contrast.

Dutch article English abstract: 50 medical-ward patients aged 70 or over; standing OH 24%, sitting post-noon-meal PPH 34%, 10% both. Parkinsonism assessed as comorbidity; no individual food comparison or PD-specific symptom estimate in abstract. Original Dutch body not recovered.

179 older residents, 4.7-year follow-up; sitting post-meal hypotension 38%, standing OH 23%; PPH adjusted mortality RR 1.79 (95% CI 1.19–2.68), PD adjustment covariate. Mortality outcome and meal unspecified, no rice or standing symptom effect; full tables not recovered.

19 levodopa-responsive Parkinsonian patients received open-label cabergoline 1 mg/day, tested with a standard meal and tilt before and during treatment. Standing BP response declined in subgroup with baseline marked PPH; abstract does not specify food or symptom severity and full tables not recovered.

10 PD and 10 controls: supine post-meal systolic drop 27 versus 8 mmHg; standing and tilt next day showed smaller orthostatic drop after lunch. No food-specific comparison or orthostatic lightheadedness estimate; existing ledger.

13 untreated PD, 11 controls: 7 PD patients had post-meal supine systolic drop greater than controls and exceeding 20% baseline; 8 had orthostatic hypotension on morning tilt and post-meal phase. No food specification or symptom rating; existing ledger.
